phases.title: Review and approve
phases.intro: Everything still waiting on your eyes or your decision. Approve each one, or send feedback. When agents change something in response, it comes back here as a new version, with your feedback shown beside it. **When every item is approved, the code freeze begins.**

phases.title: Before launch: accounts, keys and settings
phases.intro:
Work through these in any order. Each value you collect is saved here and goes into the env files at the end of this phase. Steps marked *Waits on agents* need a piece of code first; the note says which.

**One rule protects the live site.** Production keeps the keys it has now. New, separate keys go to staging, and development gets fakes. If you ever do replace a production key, the order is: push it to Netlify, ask Claude to redeploy the live site, check it works, and only then revoke the old one. All of that must finish before launch day.

phases.title: Launch day
phases.intro: In order, top to bottom. Start only after the code freeze and once every *Before launch* step is done. Allow about three hours, on a weekday morning.

phases.title: After launch
phases.intro: The checks over the following days, and the dates to remember.

sections.title: Look at staging
sections.intro: Use your iPhone where it says so. Staging is the current build: https://staging--north-foster-farm.netlify.app/

sections.title: Decisions
sections.intro: Each has a recommendation. Approving accepts the recommendation; to decide otherwise, write your answer and press **Send feedback**.

steps.title: Make a folder for this launch in your password manager
steps.body:
Create a folder (or vault) named **NFF launch**. Whenever this guide says to save something to your password manager, it goes there. Values you paste into this guide are also saved in this browser, so you can stop and come back later.

The guide has two exports at the top. **Export report for Claude** is safe to paste into the chat. **Export secrets** is a full backup of everything, including secrets. Save it as a secure note in the NFF launch folder, and never paste it anywhere else.

steps.title: Check which Netlify plan the team is on
steps.body:
Open Usage & billing, then Billing details. Note whether it says **Starter** (the older plans) or a **credit-based** plan (Free, Personal or Pro).

This matters on the credit-based Free plan: a production deploy costs 15 of 300 monthly credits, and when credits run out, every site on the team is paused. Write the plan name below so Claude can check the launch fits.

fields.label: Plan name, as Netlify shows it

steps.title: Bring in production's current values
steps.body:
Your current `.env` in the project folder is a production file: it holds the keys the live site uses. Open it in your editor, select everything, copy, and paste it into the box below. The guide reads each line and fills in the matching production fields further down: Square, PayPal, Resend, Axiom and Healthchecks. The pasted text itself isn't kept, only the values it fills in, and it never leaves this browser.

Afterwards, open the steps below; each production field should already be filled. Anything still empty is a value your `.env` didn't have, and the step says where to get it.

steps.body: Two plain values used in the staging and production files. The defaults come from your example files; change any that are wrong.

steps.title: Turn on two-factor sign-in everywhere
steps.body:
Every account that can reach a secret needs two-factor sign-in, with its recovery codes saved in the **NFF launch** folder of your password manager. Check each, and turn it on where it is off: **Netlify, GitHub, Square, PayPal, Resend, Cloudflare, Axiom, Healthchecks, UptimeRobot, Fastmail.** Any second factor works; an authenticator app or a security key is better than a text message.

Tick this when all ten are done. Claude cannot see any of them.

steps.title: Check why production's Square webhook has never succeeded
steps.body:
Production's health check shows no Square webhook delivery ever accepted. Either Square sends nothing, or every delivery fails the signature check. Find out which:
1. Open the Developer Console and open your production app.
2. In the left pane choose **Webhooks**, then **Logs**. At the top, choose **Production**.
3. Look at the **Status code** column. That's what *our* server answered, not Square. **401** means the signature check rejected it; nothing listed means nothing was sent.
4. Then open **Webhooks → Subscriptions** (Production). Check the notification URL is exactly `https://www.northfosterfarm.com/api/square/webhook`. The signature covers the URL character for character, so the bare domain, a trailing slash or `http` all break it.

Write what you found in the note on this step.

steps.body:

- **Locations:** the website's location ID.
- **Webhooks → Subscriptions:** open the production subscription, then **Show** the Signature Key.

If you fixed the subscription URL in the previous step, its signature key is unchanged.

steps.title: Make a separate Square app for staging
steps.body:
Staging gets its own application, so nothing is shared with production or development.
1. In the Developer Console, on Applications, create a new application named **NFF Staging**.
2. Set the toggle to **Sandbox**. On **Credentials**, copy the **Sandbox application ID** and **Show** the **Sandbox Access token**.
3. On **Locations** (Sandbox), copy the location ID.
4. **Webhooks → Subscriptions → Sandbox → Add subscription.** Name it "staging", with the URL below. Choose the newest API version and tick `payment.created`, `payment.updated`, `refund.created`, `refund.updated` and `order.updated`. Save, open it, and **Show** the Signature Key.
5. Optional: **Apple Pay → Add Sandbox Domain** for `staging--north-foster-farm.netlify.app`, if you want to try Apple Pay on staging (Safari only).

Note: every app under one Square login shares the same sandbox data. That's why development gets its own login in the next step.

steps.title: Add the live webhook (P2)
steps.body:
Still on the live app, scroll to **Live Webhooks** and choose **Add Webhook**. Paste the URL below, tick the events below, and save. The webhook appears in the list with an **ID**; copy it. PayPal never sends this ID in its messages, so this is the only place to get it.

Without this webhook, the site never hears about Venmo captures or refunds made in PayPal. Adding it before launch is harmless.

**Do this before the release.** Subscribe it to exactly those two events. Then set the ID on Netlify's production context as `PAYPAL_WEBHOOK_ID` (it is not a secret), deploy (a change to Netlify's environment applies only to a new deploy; see `docs/secrets.md`) and confirm it with `bin/nff env verify --production`. The live Venmo check cannot pass without it: the webhook is what finishes a Venmo payment when the browser is closed.

Under **Testing Tools → Sandbox Accounts**, open that business account and make sure it's a US account, so Venmo can appear. Save the sandbox buyer and seller logins (shown under **View/Edit Account**) in your password manager for testing.

Venmo in the sandbox is limited, and PayPal's own docs disagree about it. That's why the real proof is the live $1 payment on launch day.

Check the team name at the top left is the farm's. Open **Settings → Billing** and upgrade **Transactional** to **Pro** ($20 a month for 50,000 emails, no daily cap). Leave **Marketing** on Free while you have fewer than 1,000 contacts.

steps.title: Confirm open tracking is off
steps.body: Nothing in the code configures Resend's tracking (#189, James's decision on #244): sends carry no tracking fields and no template has a pixel. Open and click tracking are set per sending domain in Resend, not in code. Open **Domains**, the sending domain, and turn **Open Tracking** off; leave Click Tracking as you like.

steps.title: Check the Resend keys and webhook the send breaker needs
steps.body:
The send breaker (a launch blocker) stops all email and deletes the sending key if mail goes out that our code did not send, or too much of it. It needs three things in Resend.
1. **API Keys:** `RESEND_AUDIENCE_KEY` shows **Full access**. The breaker deletes the sending key with it, so this gates the rehearsal below.
2. **Webhooks:** the `/api/resend/webhook` endpoint has `email.sent`, `email.bounced` and `email.complained` ticked.
3. **The sending key's name:** Resend's key list cannot say which key is which, so the breaker finds it by name. Type the sending key's name below; it goes into `RESEND_SENDING_KEY_NAME` in `.env.production`.

Done when, after the env push and deploy, `bin/nff breaker status --production` prints "Not tripped." and no warning about sends that never came back.

fields.label: The sending key's name in Resend (RESEND_SENDING_KEY_NAME)

steps.title: See the breaker trip, and the alert reach your phone
steps.body:
Both gate launch. The breaker's alert goes out through Healthchecks and ntfy, never through Resend, so it still reaches you when mail is the thing that failed.
1. Run the rehearsal test, with a stubbed Resend and never the real key. It must pass, in particular "trips at once, deletes the sending key, alerts without Resend".
2. Run `bin/nff alert test --production`. It sends the same down push and up push the breaker sends. **Done when a down push, then an up push, reach your iPhone through ntfy.**
3. Read `bin/nff breaker status` and `bin/nff breaker reset` once, so the first real trip is not the first time you see them.

steps.title: Add the four monitors
steps.body:
For each row below, choose **+ Add New Monitor**. Pick the type shown and paste the URL. For keyword monitors, set the alert to fire when the keyword **does not exist**. Attach your phone as the alert contact, set the interval, and create.
- **HTTP(s)**, `/`, every 5 minutes.
- **Keyword**, `/order/`, keyword `id="order-form"`, every 5 minutes.
- **Keyword**, `/api/dates`, keyword `"onfarm":[`, every 5 minutes.
- **Keyword**, `/api/health`, keyword `"ok":true`, every 15 minutes.

The fifth monitor waits for launch day.

**Test:** edit the order-page monitor's keyword to something that isn't on the page. Wait for the "down" push, then put it back and wait for "up".

steps.title: Make the encryption key on your Mac
steps.body:
Backups are encrypted before they leave the site. Only your private key can open them. In Terminal on your Mac (this downloads `age` with Homebrew):
```
brew install age
mkdir -p ~/Documents/nff-keys && cd ~/Documents/nff-keys
age-keygen -o nff-backup-key.txt
chmod 600 nff-backup-key.txt
```
It prints `Public key: age1…`. Paste that public key below; it's safe to share. Then save the **whole file** `nff-backup-key.txt` in your password manager, and keep a second copy offline (a USB stick at the farm, or with Jim). The private key never goes on Netlify or into a repository. **If the private key is lost, every backup is unreadable.**

steps.title: Backblaze B2: account, bucket and key
steps.body:
1. Sign up (no card needed). Choose region **US East**, which can't be changed later.
2. **Buckets → Create a Bucket.** Name it something like `nff-backups-` plus a few random letters. Choose **Private**, leave **Object Lock off**, and create. Copy the bucket's **Endpoint**.
3. **Lifecycle Settings → Use custom lifecycle rules.** Add one rule, with no prefix: days from uploading to hiding 30, hiding to deleting 1. That matches R2's 30 days (D-189).
4. **Application Keys → Add a New Application Key.** Name it `nff-site`, allow access to that one bucket only, type **Read and Write**. Copy the **keyID** and the **applicationKey**; the second is shown only once.
5. Optional: **Caps & Alerts**, with a $1 daily cap.

steps.title: Cloudflare R2: bucket and token
steps.body:
1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, open **Storage & databases → R2** and complete the checkout to add R2. It may ask for a card; at this size it stays free.
2. **Create bucket.** Name it like the B2 one, with location hint **Eastern North America (enam)** and the Standard storage class.
3. In the bucket's **Settings → Object Lock**, turn it on and add a lock rule: Compliance mode, 30 days. Nothing can delete or overwrite a copy before then, even with the token below.
4. In **Object Lifecycle Rules → Add rule**: one rule, with no prefix, that deletes objects 30 days after they were created. Backups are kept 30 days (D-189), which is also how long deleted details can remain in them.
5. On the R2 Overview page, under **Account Details**, choose **Manage** API Tokens, then **Create Account API token**. Choose **Object Read & Write**, limit it to the one bucket, and create. R2 has no write-only token, so this one can read; that is accepted (D-EXPORT): the lock rule from step 3 stops deletes and overwrites, and the age encryption makes a read worthless. Copy the **Access Key ID**, the **Secret Access Key** (shown once) and the **S3 endpoint**, which looks like `https://<account id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com`.

Otherwise open **Project configuration → Build & deploy → Build hooks → Add build hook**, name it "staging schedule", choose the `staging` branch, and copy its URL. Production gets none, on purpose.

steps.title: Put the Netlify token in the Keychain
steps.body:
`bin/nff` reads the token from your Mac's Keychain and from no env file. Run this, then paste the new token when it asks (it stays out of your shell history):
```
security add-generic-password -a nff -s nff-netlify-auth-token -U -w
```
Then check `bin/nff --production health` works, and revoke the old token in Netlify. Remove any `NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN` line from your `.env.*` files; `bin/nff env check` fails while one is there. The `netlify` CLI keeps its own login, which the next step retires.

steps.title: Log the Netlify CLI out for good
steps.body:
The CLI's own login sits in a plain file, `~/Library/Preferences/netlify/config.json`, with the same full access as the token in your Keychain. `bin/nff` passes the Keychain token to every Netlify command, so the file is not needed.
1. Run `bin/nff --production health` once to confirm the Keychain token works.
2. Run `netlify logout`.
3. Run `ls ~/Library/Preferences/netlify/config.json`. It should say the file does not exist.

From here on, run any Netlify command as `bin/nff netlify ...`. It works after the logout. **Never run `netlify login`**; the yearly rotation changes the Keychain token only.

steps.title: Email yourself when a deploy fails
steps.body:
Open **Project configuration → Notifications → Deploy notifications → Add notification → Email notification**. Event: **Deploy failed**. Your address. Save. Add no HTTP POST and no success notice.

Netlify can't limit notifications to production, so a staging failure emails you too; a phone page for every staging failure would be noise. A small function that filters for production deploy failures and pages your phone is approved for after launch (it is on the after-launch list).

A swap later is at once, with no overlap.

steps.title: Protect the staging and main branches
steps.body:
The `lint-and-test` check exists and has run on `next` (160452a).

This makes GitHub refuse any push to `staging` or `main` whose commit hasn't passed the tests. Releases stay a fast-forward of a commit already checked.
1. Open the repository's **Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset**.
2. Name it "staging and main", and set Enforcement status to **Active**.
3. Leave the **Bypass list** empty, so administrators are included and nobody bypasses. The agents push as you, so a bypass for admins would let them skip the check.
4. **Target branches:** add `staging` and `main` by pattern.
5. **On:** Restrict deletions, Block force pushes, Require linear history.
6. **On:** Require status checks to pass. Add `lint-and-test` with source **GitHub Actions**, and leave "Require branches to be up to date before merging" **off**.
7. **Off:** Require a pull request before merging. Promotion is a fast-forward push, not a pull request.
8. Create.

Leave `next` unprotected, so lanes keep landing work. An emergency revert on `main` now goes through the tests first; `docs/rollback.md` says so.

steps.title: Make the dev@ address in Fastmail (blocking)
steps.body:
**Blocking launch gate:** deploy-failed, alert and rotation emails all go to this address, so the launch does not start without it and without the test two steps down.

In Fastmail, add the address **dev@northfosterfarm.com** (an alias on your own mailbox is enough). It receives incident steps, maintenance notices, rotation reminders and security alerts, kept apart from `FARM_NOTIFICATIONS_EMAIL`, which carries the farm's notices. The site reads it as `DEV_NOTIFICATIONS_EMAIL`, set per environment; a later step has you put it in Netlify and the env files. steps.title: Send the staging and production values to Netlify
steps.body:

```
bin/nff env push --staging
bin/nff env check --staging
netlify env:unset STAGING_TOKEN --context production
bin/nff env push --production
bin/nff env check --production
```

- **Production's first build fails the same check until production has been env pushed.** Run `bin/nff env push --production` and `bin/nff env check --production` before the release deploy, or the deploy fails and the old site stays up.
- `push` sets each key the sample lists, marks secrets as secret, skips local-only keys and never deletes anything. If it refuses because a secret is a plain variable on Netlify, mark that key secret in the Netlify UI, or run the `env:unset` commands it prints, then push again.
- `check` lists, by name only, anything that still differs. The `env:unset` lines it prints are yours to run; push never deletes.

Production's values match what it has today, so nothing changes for the live site.

steps.title: Where each value lives
steps.body:
The **NFF launch** folder in your password manager is the master copy of every value, and the only one you can read back. Netlify holds the values the site needs and the env files hold your working copies; none of those replaces the master.
- **Square, PayPal, Axiom, Healthchecks:** Netlify (production and staging contexts), your env files, the master copy.
- **Netlify token:** your Mac's Keychain and the master copy only; in no env file.
- **Staging keys:** `STAGING_TOKEN`, `E2E_STAGING_TOKEN` and the access gate's `GATE_RESEND_KEY`, `GATE_MAIL_FROM` and `GATE_TOOLBAR_EMAIL` on staging only. Never on production.
- **Resend:** production only; no staging team, key, audience or webhook. `RESEND_READ_KEY` and the old inbound secret go after launch day's live checks.
- **R2 backup token (`BACKUP_R2_*`):** Netlify production and the master copy.
- **Backup encryption key (age):** the private key lives on your Mac in `~/Documents/nff-keys` and never on Netlify. Backed up in the master copy, plus a second copy offline (a USB stick at the farm, or with Jim). Only the public key is on Netlify.
- **Backup check ping URL:** Netlify production, the master copy.
- **ntfy topic:** works like a password. Your iPhone, Healthchecks, the master copy.
- **`DEV_NOTIFICATIONS_EMAIL`:** configuration, not a secret. Netlify per environment and the env files.
- **`MAINTENANCE_SECRET`:** Netlify (a secret value) and the env files, a different one per context, and the master copy. Without it only the command line flips the switch.

3. Unblock `web.squarecdn.com`.
4. Refund the $1 with `bin/nff --production orders refund <id>`. The id is on the success card. Check the order record, Square's copy and both webhooks agree.

steps.title: Dec 1 to Jan 1: rotate the Netlify token and the yearly secrets
steps.body:
Follow `docs/secrets.md`. Rotate every secret in the window, Dec 1 to Jan 1. The Netlify and Axiom tokens expire Jan 31, a month later, so a slip costs nothing. A reminder email arrives on Dec 1 with what is due, and weekly after that until the rotation log shows it done.

**Switch maintenance mode on first, for the Square token, and do it in a quiet hour inside the window.** Square gives the old token no grace, so checkout fails between pressing Replace and the new deploy going live. Run `bin/nff --production maintenance on`, replace the token, set it on Netlify, deploy, check a payment, then run `bin/nff --production maintenance off`. Customers see the maintenance message instead of a failed payment. The other secrets rotate without downtime and need no maintenance mode.

**Keep each old credential 31 days after the new one is live** (or until its own Jan 31 expiry, whichever is first), then revoke it, and log both dates in `docs/rotation-log.md` (the second line has reason `revoked`). Exceptions: the staging tokens and the maintenance secret are swapped at once, and a leak revokes at once. The age key's old private key (both copies) is kept the same 31 days so the 30-day backup window stays readable, then destroyed.

Two design reviews, each made twice without either pass seeing the other, then merged. **Nothing is built. Every word is a draft. Build waits for your yes.** The mock-ups below are 1280 and 1500 wide, with the phone (390) noted under each area. Open them on a laptop.

## A. The places list and the cards

You said the list "seems to have no real design language at all." What the passes agreed on:
- The card leaves the map and opens in its row in the list, one open at a time. The map keeps only pins, the town outline and the tint, so no card hides another pin (today the farm's card covers the drop site's pin).
- One card, one order, for the farm, the drop site, markets and pop-ups: when, where, directions, links (only where there are any), then the shop button (the farm and the drop site only). A card omits a part and never reorders one. The kind line and the repeated name go, and so does the tiny close button; tapping the row closes it.
- Chosen means lighter, never darker: the row gets a pale wash, a 3px left bar and a filled pin glyph; the pin turns a brighter blue and is drawn last; the town gets the blue outline.
- Hovering a row lifts its pin and hovering a pin lights its row. The list scrolls inside its column.
- Keyboard and screen readers: rows are buttons; Enter or Space opens, Escape closes and returns to the row.

**Phone (390):** the list sits right under the map, and a pin tap opens its row there, scrolling it into view only if needed. No sheet over the map: at 358 by 380 a sheet would cover half of it. At 390 by 844 the map and the first rows share one screen.

Where the two passes differed, I chose: phone row, not a sheet; a pin glyph in a small circle on each row; the town on the second line, then the day ("Foster; North Scituate · Saturdays"); 36px direction chips; small labels (When, Where, Directions, More); a violet-leaning blue tint for towns.

**Questions A1 to A4.**
- **A1. The card opens in the list, not on the map.** This departs from "opens its card" if you pictured it on the map. *Recommend yes* (nothing hidden, one design, works on a phone). If no: the floating card, restyled to the same template and kept clear of other pins.
- **A2. A small pin glyph in a circle on every row.** *Recommend keep.* It points to the pin and sorts nothing, so it is not a swatch. If it reads as one to you, drop it; the wash and the bar still tie the row to its pin.
- **A3. The tint for towns with a pin is violet-leaning blue (#e4e6f4), not pure blue.** *Recommend yes*: a plain pale blue reads as a lake beside the water.
- **A4. Row wording: the town, then the day.** *Recommend as drafted.*

## B. The area right of the map, on both tabs

You called the Delivery key the one that "makes me scratch my head," with "so much empty space below it," and asked for the column 35 to 50% narrower with the map nearer the center. What the passes agreed on:
- A column stays beside the map on both tabs, the same width and top edge, so switching tabs moves nothing. It starts level with the top of the map, not the toggle (today it sits about 60px high, which is half of why it looks adrift).
- The key is a bordered card with the map's border and radius, so the two read as a pair. The Places list sits in the same card. The card is only as tall as its content; the space below reads as margin beside a map, not a hole.
- Two labeled groups in the key, since it has two independent parts: the shading (price) and the icons (what we deliver). Your wording in the rows is unchanged.
- The toggle is alone above the map; the zoom buttons sit on the map, top right, stacked. No result card, no legend on the map, and the legend stays on Delivery only.

**Phone (390):** under 992px the card goes under the map. The key becomes two side-by-side groups about 110px tall; the ZIP field and zoom stay on the map; the tag and the key fit one screen.

Where the passes differed, I chose: a 300px column (not 288px); the map capped at 608px so the whole block fits a 768px laptop window; the heading stays centered; the key heads "Shading" and "Icons"; not sticky.

**Questions B1 to B4.**
- **B1. The column is 300px, which is 32% narrower than today's 442 at 1280, not 35%.** *Recommend yes.* At 288px (35%) the longest name, "The Village Family Fitness," wraps. One value to change if you want the number. **The decision that matters most:** is a column about 300px wide, with the map and the column centered, the "narrower and more central" you meant?
- **B2. The key's two heads: "Shading" and "Icons."** *Recommend as drafted.* Alternative: "Delivery price" and "What we deliver."
- **B3. Zoom buttons top right of the map, stacked.** *Recommend yes.*
- **B4. No empty-space fix beyond the card and the narrowing.** *Recommend yes*: filling the column would mean adding the prose you cut.

## A separate small bug: the Village card's "Website"

On the Village Family Fitness pop-up card, "Website" goes to the venue's Instagram page: `data/events.json` holds an Instagram URL as `href`, and the template labels any `href` "Website." Your rule is no Instagram on a pop-up card. *Recommend:* remove the link for this event now (the mock-ups show the card without it), add an `href` only when the venue has a real website, and never show an instagram.com `href` on a pop-up. A Tour of Our New Ordering System
October 18, 2026

**Ordering from the farm online has been open for a few weeks now.** This summer was the first we sold our chicken, and we're grateful to everyone who tried it. Now you can keep buying from us after the market season ends. Here's a tour of how it works.

Ordering
The order page has eggs by the dozen, whole chickens, cuts, and sausage. What's in stock changes as we go, and the page always shows what's available now. Choose what you'd like, say how you want to get it, and pay on the page. We email you to confirm your order.

Delivery

- Order by noon on Wednesday
- As affordable as possible: $40 minimum, $5 fee

On-farm pickup

- No fee, no minimum

Drop site
- Every Saturday morning in Scituate, 10:00 to 11:00 AM
- Pick up your order for free

Your account

Farm news

After market season
Our last market of the season is the Foster Farmers Market on October 25. After that, ordering online is the way to buy from us. Our hens, although slowing down, will keep laying all year round.

This is the first version of our online ordering system, and we want to hear how it works for you. Get in touch if you run into any problems.

— James and Jim

revisions.summary: Decided. Order records are kept indefinitely for historical reporting. Personal details on an order are removed after seven years; the order keeps the date, line items, prices, totals, channel, drop site, town and ZIP, and loses the name, emails, phone and street address. A customer can delete their personal details at any time; their orders stay, re-pointed to a deleted-household record (Null Object pattern), and deletion is final (a returning customer starts a new household, with no restore or re-link). Data export (download everything NFF holds) is planned after deletion ships, not before. Quiet accounts are never deleted automatically; after one year without interaction the household is unsubscribed from marketing mail and sent one transactional notice about how to delete if they'd like to. Signing in, an action while signed in, a badge-scanned market sale, or a click on a link in an email resets the one-year clock; an unsubscribe click or a visit only to opt out, change settings or delete does not. Email open tracking stays off permanently in Resend and every template; click and conversion tracking are fine. Nothing open in retention itself; the #189 spec can proceed. Data export (step two) needs its own spec later.

The stage slides sideways. One target only and the clearest wording, but a label, not a fill, says which pane is open.
